cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What makes a kernel-enforced agent sandbox different from a prompt-based or tool-logic restriction?
cards.answer: The boundary is held by OS kernel primitives beneath the agent, inherited by every process it spawns — so a prompt-injected or misbehaving agent can't negotiate its way out, it can only run into the wall.

cards.heading: Filesystem isolation
cards.question: How does the filesystem layer stay safe even under a broad directory grant?
cards.answer: Access defaults to deny (ungranted paths don't exist from inside the sandbox), the working directory is read-only until opted in, and dotfiles are masked even when a whole directory is granted — so granting a home directory doesn't hand over SSH keys or credential files.

cards.heading: Network isolation rationale
cards.question: What is the design rationale behind the network layer's default-deny egress proxy?
cards.answer: Exfiltration needs a destination — an allow-list of methods, hosts and paths (with private ranges and cloud metadata endpoints blocked) bounds the damage of a successful injection instead of trying to detect the injection itself.

cards.heading: Credential injection
cards.question: How does credential injection let an agent use a secret it can never read?
cards.answer: The agent holds only a placeholder token; the proxy substitutes the real secret solely on requests that already match the allow-list — only the placeholder ever reaches logs, transcripts and model context, so a leaked placeholder is inert off the proxy.

cards.heading: The general rule
cards.question: What general principle does this sandbox design encode about where controls should live?
cards.answer: A control an agent can be talked out of is not a control — enforcement has to sit beneath the agent, in the kernel, not inside its own reasoning or tool logic.
